# Exercise 8: Multilevel regression {.unnumbered}

In Exercise 7 we fit a single regression line to all the data at once. But many real datasets have **group structure**: measurements come from different subjects, sites, batches, or schools, and each group may behave somewhat differently. A multilevel (or *hierarchical*) model treats each group as having its own parameters, while tying those parameters together through a shared prior whose hyperparameters are themselves learned from the data. This produces **partial pooling**: groups with little data borrow strength from the global pattern, while groups with lots of data are allowed to deviate. We will:

- fit three regressions — **complete pooling**, **no pooling**, and **partial pooling** — and contrast their estimates,
- standardize the inputs and switch between **centered** and **non-centered** parametrizations to study how model specification affects MCMC geometry,
- use **posterior predictive checks** to criticize each model at the group level,
- compare the three models with **leave-one-out cross-validation** and on a held-out set of real observations.

The dataset is the classic `sleepstudy` from @BelenkySleepDoseResponse2003, in which 18 subjects had their sleep restricted to 3 hours per night for 9 nights and their reaction times measured daily on a psychomotor vigilance task.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-fold: false
#| code-summary: "Required imports"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

import jax
from jax import random
import jax.numpy as jnp

import numpyro
import numpyro.distributions as dist
from numpyro.infer import MCMC, NUTS, Predictive

import arviz as az

rng_key = random.PRNGKey(42)
```


## The data

The `sleepstudy` dataset records the average reaction time (in milliseconds) on a 10-minute psychomotor vigilance task for each of 18 subjects on each of 10 consecutive days. Day 0 is a baseline night with normal sleep; from Day 2 onward subjects were restricted to 3 hours of sleep per night, and reaction times were measured at the end of each day. To make the multilevel structure more interesting, we use a version of the data in which some subjects have all 10 measurements, others only 5, and a few only 2.

Load the data from [data/exercise-8/sleepstudy_processed.csv](../data/exercise-8/sleepstudy_processed.csv):

```{python}
#| label: load-data
#| code-fold: false
df = pd.read_csv("../data/exercise-8/sleepstudy_processed.csv")

day = jnp.array(df["day"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.float32)
reaction = jnp.array(df["reaction"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.float32)
subject = jnp.array(df["subject_idx"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.int32)

subject_ids = sorted(df["subject"].unique().tolist())
n_subjects = int(df["subject_idx"].nunique())
n_obs = len(df)
n_subjects, n_obs
```

The columns are `subject` (the original numeric id), `subject_idx` (a contiguous integer index $j \in \{0, \ldots, J-1\}$ that we will use to gather per-subject parameters), `day`, and `reaction`. There are $J = 18$ subjects and $N = 110$ observations in total.

**Task 0 — Visualize the per-subject trends.** Plot reaction time vs. day for each subject, with the best-fit line through each subject's points overlaid. What features do you notice that a single global regression would miss? What do you expect the per-subject lines to look like for the subjects with only 2 observations?

You can fit a line through each subject's points with [`jnp.polyfit`](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.numpy.polyfit.html), passing `deg=1` to obtain the slope and intercept.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-data
#| fig-cap: "Reaction time (ms) vs. day for each of the 18 subjects, with a best-fit line through overlaid."
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 4, figsize=(7, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
day_grid = jnp.linspace(0, 9, 50)

for j, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    if j >= n_subjects:
        ax.axis("off")
        continue
    mask = subject == j
    xs = day[mask]
    ys = reaction[mask]
    slope, intercept = jnp.polyfit(xs, ys, 1)
    ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=15, color="black", alpha=0.7)
    ax.plot(day_grid, intercept + slope * day_grid, color="C1", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.set_title(f"Subject {subject_ids[j]} (n={int(mask.sum())})", fontsize=8)

for ax in axes[-1, :]:
    ax.set_xlabel("Day")
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("Reaction (ms)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Most subjects with enough observations show a positive trend: as the days of sleep restriction accumulate, reaction times rise. But the *amount* of degradation varies substantially across subjects, and baseline reaction times also differ markedly. A single global regression line would average these very different trajectories into a moderate slope that fits no individual particularly well.

For the subjects with only 2 observations, the line is an *interpolation* rather than a fit — it passes exactly through both points by construction — and is therefore at the mercy of their noise: a single noisy measurement can flip the slope from steep to flat or even negative. We will see that this is precisely the situation in which partial pooling helps.

:::


## Standardizing the data

Before fitting any model, it pays to put the predictor and the response on a common, **unit-free scale**. We do this by *standardizing* (also called *z-scoring*): for each variable $v$ we subtract the sample mean and divide by the sample standard deviation,
$$
z_v = \frac{v - \bar{v}}{\text{sd}(v)},
$$
so that $z_v$ has mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$. We will fit our models on the standardized scale, and back-transform when we want to report results in the original units (milliseconds and days).

```{python}
#| label: standardize
#| code-fold: false
day_mean, day_std = day.mean(), day.std()
reaction_mean, reaction_std = reaction.mean(), reaction.std()

z_day = (day - day_mean) / day_std
z_reaction = (reaction - reaction_mean) / reaction_std
```

We keep the four constants `day_mean`, `day_std`, `reaction_mean`, `reaction_std` so that we can later un-standardize the model's predictions: a posterior draw $z_y$ on the standardized scale corresponds to $y = \bar{y} + \text{sd}(y) \cdot z_y$ on the original scale.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why standardize?"}

Standardization helps in two ways: it makes priors easier to choose, and it makes the posterior easier for MCMC to explore.

**Priors become easier to set.** On the standardized scale, both predictor and response have unit standard deviation by construction, so a $\text{Normal}(0, 1)$ prior on slopes and intercepts is automatically *weakly informative* in the sense of @sec-priors: it allows the data to speak while ruling out absurdly extreme values. The same prior recipe transports across datasets, since the units have been removed.

**The posterior geometry becomes nicer.** When the predictor is centered, the posterior correlation between the intercept and the slope is greatly reduced. This is because moving the slope no longer drags the intercept along by a large lever arm. Less correlated posteriors are easier for MCMC to explore because they don't have narrow ridges or funnels that are tricky to navigate.
:::


## Part 1: Three pooling regimes

We will fit three regression models that differ only in how they treat the per-subject parameters: **complete pooling** (one global line), **no pooling** (one independent line per subject), and **partial pooling** (per-subject lines tied together by a shared prior). In each subtask below we state the model mathematically and then translate it into NumPyro code.

Throughout we use $i = 1, \ldots, N$ for observations and $j = 1, \ldots, J$ for subjects, and write $j[i]$ for the subject of the $i$-th observation. All three models use the standardized variables $x_i = z_{\text{day},i}$ and $y_i = z_{\text{reaction},i}$, and share a common call signature:

```python
def model_*(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects): ...
```

Each model records the conditional mean with `numpyro.deterministic("mu", ...)` and ends with `numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu, sigma), obs=y)`, so the same function generates fake data when `y=None` and conditions on data when `y` is provided. The keyword argument `n_subjects=n_subjects` captures the value computed in the *Data* section as a default, so we don't have to pass it explicitly to `mcmc.run`, `Predictive`, or `log_likelihood` — handy because those calls happen many times below.

### Task 1a — Complete pooling

Ignore subject identity entirely: one global intercept and slope describe everyone.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) \\
\beta &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha + \beta \, x_i \\
y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

This is just a Gaussian linear regression and serves as a baseline: if subject identity does not matter, this simple model will do as well as any.

Write `model_pooled(x, subject, y=None)`. The argument `subject` is unused here but kept for a uniform signature.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: model-pooled
#| code-fold: false
def model_pooled(x, subject, y=None):
    alpha = numpyro.sample("alpha", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    beta = numpyro.sample("beta", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    sigma = numpyro.sample("sigma", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    mu = numpyro.deterministic("mu", alpha + beta * x)
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu, sigma), obs=y)
```

:::

### Task 1b — No pooling

Each subject gets its own independent intercept and slope, with no information shared between subjects.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_j &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1), \quad j = 1, \ldots, J \\
\beta_j &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1), \quad j = 1, \ldots, J \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_{j[i]} \, x_i \\
y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the opposite extreme: each subject is fit independently, as if the other subjects did not exist. It captures the per-subject variation but cannot generalize to a new subject, and overfits subjects with very few observations.

Write `model_unpooled(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects)` with one $(\alpha_j, \beta_j)$ pair per subject.

The per-subject parameters form a vector of $J$ independent draws from the same prior. This kind of structure can be represented in NumPyro using a **plate**. See the box below for a quick introduction. Once you have $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ as length-$J$ vectors, gather the right entries for each observation with array indexing: `alpha_j[subject]` produces a length-$N$ vector containing the intercept of the subject for each row.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Background: NumPyro plates"}

A `numpyro.plate(name, size)` is a context manager that turns a single `numpyro.sample` call into independent draws of length `size`. The plate corresponds to plate notation for diagrams introduced in @sec-implement-numpyro. The line

```python
with numpyro.plate("subjects", n_subjects):
    alpha_j = numpyro.sample("alpha_j", dist.Normal(0, 1))
```

draws a vector of i.i.d. $\text{Normal}(0, 1)$ values of length `n_subjects` and registers them as a single inference site named `"alpha_j"`. You can have multiple `sample` statements inside the same plate. They are vectorized over the same axis.

**Why not just a `for` loop?** The same model could be written without a plate as

```python
alpha_j = []

for j in range(n_subjects):
    alpha_j.append(numpyro.sample(f"alpha_{j}", dist.Normal(0, 1)))

alpha_j = jnp.stack(alpha_j)
```

This loop creates `n_subjects` separate sample sites, each with its own scalar distribution. However, this runs much slower than a single vectorized sample inside a plate, and it also creates a more cluttered trace with many more sites to keep track of. Whenever you want to use a for loop to create multiple independent parameters, it's a sign that you should be using a plate instead.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: model-unpooled
#| code-fold: false
def model_unpooled(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects):
    with numpyro.plate("subjects", n_subjects):
        alpha_j = numpyro.sample("alpha_j", dist.Normal(0, 1))
        beta_j = numpyro.sample("beta_j", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    sigma = numpyro.sample("sigma", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    mu = numpyro.deterministic("mu", alpha_j[subject] + beta_j[subject] * x)
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu, sigma), obs=y)
```

:::

### Task 1c — Partial pooling

Each subject still has its own $(\alpha_j, \beta_j)$, but they are drawn from a common prior whose location and scale are themselves inferred. Subjects with few or noisy observations are pulled (*shrunk*) toward the population means.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_\alpha, \mu_\beta &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) \\
\tau_\alpha, \tau_\beta &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\alpha_j &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\alpha, \tau_\alpha), \quad j = 1, \ldots, J \\
\beta_j &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\beta, \tau_\beta), \quad j = 1, \ldots, J \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_{j[i]} \, x_i \\
y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

The hyperparameters $\mu_\alpha$ and $\mu_\beta$ describe the *population-level* intercept and slope — what we would expect for an average new subject — and $\tau_\alpha$, $\tau_\beta$ describe how much subjects vary around them. The model uses the data from all subjects to learn these, then uses them as a prior on each individual $\alpha_j, \beta_j$.

Write `model_partial(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects)`. The structure is the same as `model_unpooled`, but the priors on $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ now use the learned hyperparameters $(\mu_\alpha, \tau_\alpha)$ and $(\mu_\beta, \tau_\beta)$ instead of fixed $(0, 1)$. Sample the hyperparameters *outside* the plate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: model-partial-centered
#| code-fold: false
def model_partial(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects):
    mu_alpha = numpyro.sample("mu_alpha", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    mu_beta = numpyro.sample("mu_beta", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    tau_alpha = numpyro.sample("tau_alpha", dist.Exponential(1.0))
    tau_beta = numpyro.sample("tau_beta", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    with numpyro.plate("subjects", n_subjects):
        alpha_j = numpyro.sample("alpha_j", dist.Normal(mu_alpha, tau_alpha))
        beta_j = numpyro.sample("beta_j", dist.Normal(mu_beta, tau_beta))
    sigma = numpyro.sample("sigma", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    mu = numpyro.deterministic("mu", alpha_j[subject] + beta_j[subject] * x)
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu, sigma), obs=y)
```

When you suspect a shape bug — common when wiring per-subject parameters — the *Debugging models* technique from @sec-implement-numpyro is invaluable: trace the model once with `numpyro.handlers.seed` + `numpyro.handlers.trace` and inspect the shape of every site. Here we use it to confirm that the per-subject parameters are length-$J$ and `mu` is length-$N$:

```{python}
#| label: trace-shapes
#| code-fold: false
with numpyro.handlers.seed(rng_seed=0):
    trace = numpyro.handlers.trace(model_partial).get_trace(
        x=z_day, subject=subject, y=None
    )

for name, site in trace.items():
    print(f"{name:>10s}  shape={tuple(site['value'].shape)}")
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Aside: centered vs. non-centered parametrization"}

The model above is the **centered** parametrization: each $\alpha_j$ is drawn directly from $\text{Normal}(\mu_\alpha, \tau_\alpha)$, so the prior on $\alpha_j$ depends on the values of the hyperparameters. An algebraically equivalent way to write the same model introduces a standardized auxiliary variable and reconstructs $\alpha_j$ as a deterministic transform:

$$
z_j^\alpha \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1), \qquad \alpha_j = \mu_\alpha + \tau_\alpha \, z_j^\alpha,
$$

and analogously for $\beta_j$. By the change-of-variables rule the two formulations encode the same Bayesian model, so the resulting posteriors over $(\mu_\alpha, \tau_\alpha, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_J)$ are identical.

What is *not* identical is the geometry that NUTS sees. NUTS samples the latent variables the model registers — $\alpha_j$ in one case, $z_j^\alpha$ in the other. In the centered version the posterior of $(\log \tau_\alpha, \alpha_j)$ has a *funnel* shape: small $\tau_\alpha$ pinches the $\alpha_j$ near $\mu_\alpha$, large $\tau_\alpha$ lets them spread out, and a single step size cannot fit both regions. In the non-centered version $z_j^\alpha$ is sampled from a fixed unit Normal regardless of $\tau_\alpha$, removing the funnel from the latent geometry.

```python
def model_partial_nc(x, subject, y=None, n_subjects=n_subjects):
    mu_alpha = numpyro.sample("mu_alpha", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    mu_beta = numpyro.sample("mu_beta", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    tau_alpha = numpyro.sample("tau_alpha", dist.Exponential(1.0))
    tau_beta = numpyro.sample("tau_beta", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    with numpyro.plate("subjects", n_subjects):
        z_alpha = numpyro.sample("z_alpha", dist.Normal(0, 1))
        z_beta = numpyro.sample("z_beta", dist.Normal(0, 1))
    sigma = numpyro.sample("sigma", dist.Exponential(1.0))

    alpha_j = numpyro.deterministic("alpha_j", mu_alpha + tau_alpha * z_alpha)
    beta_j = numpyro.deterministic("beta_j", mu_beta + tau_beta * z_beta)

    mu = numpyro.deterministic("mu", alpha_j[subject] + beta_j[subject] * x)
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu, sigma), obs=y)
```

The non-centered form is the safer default for hierarchical models, especially when the data are sparse or the population scales $\tau$ are small. For `sleepstudy` the funnel is mild — both parametrizations fit fine and produce essentially identical diagnostics — so we stick with the centered version `model_partial` in the remainder of the exercise.

:::


## Part 2: Inference

We now run NUTS on each of the three models and inspect the diagnostics. To avoid repeating boilerplate, we wrap the inference in a small helper that runs four chains and returns an ArviZ `InferenceData` object. We use 1000 warmup and 2000 sampling iterations per chain. We pass `log_likelihood=True` to `az.from_numpyro` so that the per-observation log-likelihood at every posterior draw gets attached to the `InferenceData` — we will need it for the model comparison in Part 5.

```{python}
#| label: run-mcmc-helper
#| code-fold: false
def run_mcmc(model, rng_key, **model_kwargs):
    kernel = NUTS(model)
    mcmc = MCMC(
        kernel,
        num_warmup=1000,
        num_samples=2000,
        num_chains=4,
        progress_bar=False,
    )
    mcmc.run(rng_key, **model_kwargs)
    idata = az.from_numpyro(mcmc, log_likelihood=True)
    return mcmc, idata
```

We split the master `rng_key` once so each fit uses a fresh sub-key:

```{python}
#| label: run-all
#| code-fold: false
k_pooled, k_unpooled, k_partial = random.split(rng_key, 3)
data_kwargs = dict(x=z_day, subject=subject, y=z_reaction)

mcmc_pooled, idata_pooled = run_mcmc(model_pooled, k_pooled, **data_kwargs)
mcmc_unpooled, idata_unpooled = run_mcmc(model_unpooled, k_unpooled, **data_kwargs)
mcmc_partial, idata_partial = run_mcmc(model_partial, k_partial, **data_kwargs)
```

**Task 2 — Diagnose convergence.** For each fit, call `az.summary` on the top-level parameters and check that $\hat{R} \le 1.01$ and that the effective sample sizes `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail` are at least a few hundred.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: summary-pooled
#| code-fold: false
az.summary(idata_pooled, var_names=["alpha", "beta", "sigma"])
```

```{python}
#| label: summary-unpooled
#| code-fold: false
az.summary(idata_unpooled, var_names=["alpha_j", "beta_j", "sigma"])
```

```{python}
#| label: summary-partial
#| code-fold: false
az.summary(
    idata_partial,
    var_names=["mu_alpha", "mu_beta", "tau_alpha", "tau_beta", "sigma"],
)
```

All three fits give $\hat{R} \approx 1.00$ and ESS values in the thousands, so we can trust the posterior summaries.

:::


## Part 3: Shrinkage

The defining behaviour of partial pooling is **shrinkage**: each per-subject slope $\beta_j$ is pulled toward the population mean $\mu_\beta$ by an amount that depends on how much the data say about subject $j$. Subjects with many observations and a clear trend stay close to their no-pooling estimate; subjects with few observations or noisy data get pulled in much more strongly. We can see both effects directly by comparing the per-subject slopes under no pooling and partial pooling.

**Task 3 — Forest plot of shrinkage.** For each subject, plot the posterior mean and 89% credible interval of $\beta_j$ under both the no-pooling and partial-pooling fits, side by side. Add a vertical line at the posterior mean of the population slope $\mu_\beta$ from the partial-pooling fit. Sort subjects so the pattern of shrinkage is easy to read, and pay attention to subjects with only 2 observations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint: extracting per-subject summaries"}

Calling `mcmc.get_samples()` returns a dictionary of JAX arrays whose first axis stacks all chains and draws together. For example, `mcmc_unpooled.get_samples()["beta_j"]` has shape `(num_chains * num_samples, J)`. Reduce along axis 0 with `jnp.mean` and `jnp.quantile` to get length-$J$ vectors of posterior means and credible-interval bounds:

```python
samples_unp = mcmc_unpooled.get_samples()
beta_unp = samples_unp["beta_j"]                          # shape (S, J)
mean_unp = jnp.mean(beta_unp, axis=0)                     # shape (J,)
lo_unp, hi_unp = jnp.quantile(beta_unp, jnp.array([0.055, 0.945]), axis=0)
```

Use the same pattern for `mcmc_partial`. The population mean is `jnp.mean(mcmc_partial.get_samples()["mu_beta"])`.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Per-subject slopes $\\beta_j$ on the standardized scale under no-pooling (orange) and partial-pooling (blue) fits, with 89% credible intervals. The vertical line marks the partial-pooling population mean $\\mu_\\beta$. Subjects are sorted by their no-pooling estimate, and the count $n_j$ of observations is shown on the right."
#| code-fold: true
def per_subject_summary(samples, name):
    arr = samples[name]                                       # shape (S, J)
    mean = jnp.mean(arr, axis=0)
    lo, hi = jnp.quantile(arr, jnp.array([0.055, 0.945]), axis=0)
    return mean, lo, hi

samples_unp = mcmc_unpooled.get_samples()
samples_par = mcmc_partial.get_samples()

mean_unp, lo_unp, hi_unp = per_subject_summary(samples_unp, "beta_j")
mean_par, lo_par, hi_par = per_subject_summary(samples_par, "beta_j")
mu_beta_hat = float(jnp.mean(samples_par["mu_beta"]))

n_obs_per_subject = jnp.array(
    [int((subject == j).sum()) for j in range(n_subjects)]
)

# Sort subjects by no-pooling estimate.
order = jnp.argsort(mean_unp)
y_pos = jnp.arange(n_subjects)
offset = 0.18

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.errorbar(
    mean_unp[order], y_pos + offset,
    xerr=jnp.stack([mean_unp[order] - lo_unp[order], hi_unp[order] - mean_unp[order]]),
    fmt="o", color="C1", label="no pooling", capsize=2, markersize=4,
)
ax.errorbar(
    mean_par[order], y_pos - offset,
    xerr=jnp.stack([mean_par[order] - lo_par[order], hi_par[order] - mean_par[order]]),
    fmt="o", color="C0", label="partial pooling", capsize=2, markersize=4,
)
ax.axvline(mu_beta_hat, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label=r"$\mu_\beta$")

ax.set_yticks(y_pos.tolist())
ax.set_yticklabels(
    [f"Subject {subject_ids[int(j)]} (n={int(n_obs_per_subject[int(j)])})"
     for j in order],
    fontsize=8,
)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\beta_j$ (standardized scale)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two patterns stand out. First, the partial-pooling estimates sit closer to the dashed line $\mu_\beta$ than the no-pooling estimates do — the per-subject slopes are pulled toward the population mean. Second, the shrinkage is *not* uniform: it is strongest precisely for the subjects with only 2 observations (whose no-pooling slopes are at the mercy of two noisy points) and weakest for subjects with 10 observations and a clear trend. The credible intervals also tighten considerably under partial pooling, because each subject now also benefits from the information the other subjects provide about plausible slope values.

:::


## Part 4: Posterior predictive checks

Diagnostics like $\hat R$ and ESS only tell us that MCMC converged, not whether the model is a good description of the data. For that we use **posterior predictive checks** (PPCs): we draw fake data from the fitted model and compare it to the real data. If the two look similar, the model can reproduce the patterns we care about; if not, the discrepancy tells us how the model fails.

Concretely, for each posterior draw $(\alpha^{(s)}, \beta^{(s)}, \sigma^{(s)})$ we generate a replicated dataset $\tilde y^{(s)}$ from the likelihood at the *observed* predictors $x_i$ and subject indices $j[i]$. Stacking these gives a posterior predictive sample $\tilde y \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times N}$. NumPyro provides the `Predictive` class for exactly this purpose — given posterior samples and the model, it runs the model forward in batched mode.

**Task 4 — Per-subject posterior predictive checks.** For each of the three models, draw posterior predictive reaction times at the observed $(x_i, j[i])$, back-transform to the original millisecond scale, and overlay the per-subject observed scatter with the posterior mean line and an 89% predictive band. What kind of mismatch does each model show?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint: drawing posterior predictives with `Predictive`"}

`Predictive(model, posterior_samples=samples)` returns a callable that runs the model once per posterior draw, conditioning on the supplied samples and re-sampling everything else. Pass `y=None` so that the `"obs"` site is sampled rather than conditioned on:

```python
predictive = Predictive(model_partial, posterior_samples=mcmc_partial.get_samples())
ppc = predictive(rng_key_pp, x=z_day, subject=subject, y=None)
y_rep = ppc["obs"]   # shape (S, N), on the standardized scale
```

To get back to milliseconds: `y_rep_ms = reaction_mean + reaction_std * y_rep`.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

We loop over the three models, generating posterior predictive draws on the standardized scale and immediately un-standardizing them.

```{python}
#| label: posterior-predictive
#| code-fold: false
k_pp_pooled, k_pp_unpooled, k_pp_partial = random.split(random.PRNGKey(0), 3)

def posterior_predictive(model, mcmc, rng_key_pp):
    predictive = Predictive(model, posterior_samples=mcmc.get_samples())
    ppc = predictive(rng_key_pp, x=z_day, subject=subject, y=None)
    return reaction_mean + reaction_std * ppc["obs"]   # shape (S, N), milliseconds

y_rep_pooled = posterior_predictive(model_pooled, mcmc_pooled, k_pp_pooled)
y_rep_unpooled = posterior_predictive(model_unpooled, mcmc_unpooled, k_pp_unpooled)
y_rep_partial = posterior_predictive(model_partial, mcmc_partial, k_pp_partial)
```

For each subject we summarize the predictive distribution at each observed day by its mean and 5%/95% quantiles, then overlay the observed scatter:

```{python}
#| label: fig-ppc
#| fig-cap: "Per-subject posterior predictive checks. Black dots are the observed reaction times; the line is the posterior mean prediction and the shaded band the 89% predictive interval. Complete pooling uses one global line for everyone, no pooling fits each subject independently, and partial pooling shares strength across subjects."
#| code-fold: true
def ppc_summary(y_rep):
    mean = jnp.mean(y_rep, axis=0)
    lo, hi = jnp.quantile(y_rep, jnp.array([0.055, 0.945]), axis=0)
    return mean, lo, hi

models_to_plot = [
    ("Complete pooling", y_rep_pooled, "C2"),
    ("No pooling", y_rep_unpooled, "C1"),
    ("Partial pooling", y_rep_partial, "C0"),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    len(models_to_plot), n_subjects,
    figsize=(14, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True,
)

for row, (title, y_rep, color) in enumerate(models_to_plot):
    mean_pred, lo_pred, hi_pred = ppc_summary(y_rep)
    for j in range(n_subjects):
        ax = axes[row, j]
        mask = subject == j
        order = jnp.argsort(day[mask])
        xs = day[mask][order]
        ax.fill_between(xs, lo_pred[mask][order], hi_pred[mask][order],
                        color=color, alpha=0.25)
        ax.plot(xs, mean_pred[mask][order], color=color, linewidth=1.2)
        ax.scatter(day[mask], reaction[mask], s=10, color="black", alpha=0.8)
        if row == 0:
            ax.set_title(f"S{subject_ids[j]}", fontsize=8)
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(title, fontsize=9)

for ax in axes[-1, :]:
    ax.set_xlabel("Day")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each model produces a visually different fit:

- **Complete pooling** draws the *same* line for every subject, since it has no notion of subject identity. Subjects with steep degradation are systematically under-predicted, and subjects with flat trajectories are over-predicted. The 89% band is wide because a single $\sigma$ has to absorb all the between-subject variation as if it were noise.
- **No pooling** fits each subject's points snugly — the line goes through the cloud and the band is narrow. But for the subjects with only 2 observations the line is essentially an interpolation through two noisy points: the slope is over-confident and would generalize poorly to a third measurement on the same subject.
- **Partial pooling** is a compromise. Subjects with plenty of data get a line very close to the no-pooling fit; subjects with only 2 observations get a line and band that are visibly pulled toward the population trend, with a wider predictive band that honestly reflects the uncertainty.

:::


## Part 5: Model comparison

The PPCs gave a qualitative picture of how the three models fit. To put a number on it, we now compare them by their **expected out-of-sample predictive accuracy** — how well each model would predict a *new* observation from the same data-generating process. The gold standard is leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO): for every observation $y_i$, refit the model without that point and score the held-out point, then sum the scores. Refitting $N$ times is expensive, but ArviZ approximates LOO directly from the existing posterior samples using **Pareto-smoothed importance sampling** (PSIS-LOO), so we get the comparison essentially for free.

Concretely, `az.compare` ranks models by their **expected log pointwise predictive density** (`elpd_loo`, higher is better) together with a standard error and the differences between models. It uses the per-observation log-likelihoods that our `run_mcmc` helper already attached to each `idata`.

To complement this leave-one-out estimate, we will also evaluate the models on **genuinely held-out data**. Recall that we artificially thinned the original `sleepstudy` dataset to make some subjects sparse — the dropped rows are real observations from the same experiment, sitting in [`sleepstudy_heldout.csv`](../data/exercise-8/sleepstudy_heldout.csv) (70 rows from the 11 subjects with $n_j < 10$). We will reuse the posteriors from Part 2 (already fit on exactly the training rows) and score the test points by their expected log predictive density,
$$
\text{ELPD}_{\text{test}} = \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \log \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} p\bigl(y_i^{\text{test}} \mid x_i^{\text{test}}, \theta^{(s)}\bigr).
$$

This is the same quantity as `elpd_loo`, with two differences: the conditioning posterior is the full-data posterior rather than the leave-one-out one, and the sum is over a real test set rather than over the training points themselves.

**Task 5 — Compare the three models.** First call `az.compare({name: idata})` and inspect the LOO ranking. Then load the held-out CSV, standardize it with the *training* mean and std, and compute $\text{ELPD}_{\text{test}}$ for each of the three fits. Which model is preferred under each criterion, and do the two criteria agree?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| label: loo-compare
#| code-fold: false
az.compare(
    {"pooled": idata_pooled, "unpooled": idata_unpooled, "partial": idata_partial}
)
```

Complete pooling lands far below the other two: a single global line cannot capture the per-subject variation, and LOO penalizes it heavily. The no-pooling and partial-pooling models are essentially tied on `elpd_loo`, and both produce Pareto-$\hat k$ warnings — observations whose leave-one-out posterior is too different from the full posterior for importance sampling to be reliable. The flagged points are precisely the $n_j = 2$ subjects, where dropping one of the two points genuinely changes the fit a lot.

When PSIS-LOO is unreliable or two models tie, evaluating on truly held-out data gives a clean tiebreaker:

```{python}
#| label: held-out-elpd
#| code-fold: false
from numpyro.infer.util import log_likelihood

df_test = pd.read_csv("../data/exercise-8/sleepstudy_heldout.csv")
x_test = (jnp.array(df_test["day"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.float32) - day_mean) / day_std
y_test = (jnp.array(df_test["reaction"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.float32) - reaction_mean) / reaction_std
subj_test = jnp.array(df_test["subject_idx"].to_numpy(), dtype=jnp.int32)
test_kwargs = dict(x=x_test, subject=subj_test, y=y_test)

def held_out_elpd(model, mcmc):
    # Drop the deterministic `mu` site: its stored shape matches the training
    # data and would otherwise clash with the test predictors.
    samples = {k: v for k, v in mcmc.get_samples().items() if k != "mu"}
    log_lik = log_likelihood(model, samples, **test_kwargs)["obs"]    # (S, n_test)
    pointwise = jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(log_lik, axis=0) - jnp.log(log_lik.shape[0])
    return float(pointwise.sum())

{
    "pooled":   held_out_elpd(model_pooled,   mcmc_pooled),
    "unpooled": held_out_elpd(model_unpooled, mcmc_unpooled),
    "partial":  held_out_elpd(model_partial,  mcmc_partial),
}
```

On genuinely new observations partial pooling wins clearly. The unpooled model overfits each subject's training points — its narrow per-subject posterior places too little mass near a held-out value that lies on the noisy side. Partial pooling pulls each subject's slope and intercept toward the population, giving a wider, better-calibrated predictive distribution. This is the same intuition the PPCs and the shrinkage plot suggested, now expressed as a single number per model.

:::
